albums.title: Noise canceller v0.13.2: save, close, reopen
albums.description: Travis asked whether learned profiles survive save, close REAPER, reopen. New regression test: the plugin state is saved mid-take, loaded into a fresh instance, and its setup code runs again after loading (REAPER sometimes does that), then the output is compared with a run that never closed.
albums.result: The profile survives in all three modes, with auto and manual learn, at 44.1/48/96 kHz: no re-learn, no mute, output within -57 to -72 dB of the never-closed run. Found and fixed: the 'let harmonics fade out' A/B switch held harmonics fully open in a reopened project until any slider moved (a value computed in the wrong order). Default sound unchanged. Also fixed a test-harness bug (ysfx dropped the A/B switch settings on save; REAPER itself doesn't). Untested without REAPER: if the plugin learns while its window is closed, REAPER may not ask to save on close; an explicit save still keeps the profile.

albums.title: Noise canceller: port scaffolding and licensing
albums.description: Ready for the C++ port once the sound passes Travis's listen. An iPlug2 project builds the plugin as VST3 and CLAP on Windows around a framework-free DSP core, which passes audio through for now. Every shipped dependency's license file was checked for GPL and for costs.
albums.result: VST3 passes Steinberg's validator (47 tests passed, 0 failed); the CLAP loads and reports the right id, name and features. Licenses: all permissive (iPlug2/WDL zlib, VST3 SDK MIT since 3.8 in Oct 2025, CLAP MIT, NanoVG zlib, Yoga MIT). No GPL ships: the standalone app isn't built because it would compile Steinberg's ASIO files (GPLv3 or a signed agreement). Cost for Windows VST3+CLAP: nothing. Mac/AU (Apple, $99/yr) and AAX (iLok + Avid registration) are later and optional. Not yet loaded in REAPER.

albums.title: Noise canceller: harmonic protection, tested and dropped
albums.description: Idea: find the notes from the clean low band and protect their harmonics up top, so the 12 dB threshold stops eating the guitar's top end. Tested on all 205 guitar takes from 2024 (24 min of playing; old room, so near-clean in the top end) mixed with the in-game interference. The filter was emulated in Python and given a perfect pitch tracker: the clean take's actual partial positions. Its trade-off was compared with simply lowering the threshold.
albums.result: The top end is mostly harmonic (72% of 2.5-10 kHz energy on partials), but protecting the partials lands on the same curve as the Noise threshold dial, or 0.2-0.5 dB under it, at every window from 6 to 46 ms. Reason: a bin where a partial sits under the noise also passes that noise; only finer frequency resolution separates them. A 46 ms window keeps ~4 dB more top end at the same cut: too slow to play through, possible for re-amping recorded DIs. Also measured: 2024 takes' top-end floor is ~58 dB under in-game noise; from Sept 2025 (new room) the floor is 15-20 dB higher.

albums.title: Noise canceller v0.13.1: crisp pick attacks (A/B)
albums.description: A fourth A/B switch, built blind while Travis is away from the rig. Under in-game noise the 12 dB threshold softens the first milliseconds of every pick and takes most of its click above 2 kHz. Cause: the filter's smoothed (decision-directed) estimate opens a bin over several frames. A 3 ms lookahead alone changed nothing. With the switch on, for 20 ms after a guitar-like pick a bin may open at once to its own level. No added latency; default Off.
albums.result: Switch off: bit-identical to v0.13 in every mode. Switch on: first 3 ms of picks -4.6 -> -3.0 dB, guitar 4-8 kHz kept -37 -> -17 dB, 8-16 kHz -25 -> -10 dB. Costs: sparkles 0.1 -> 2.2/s on a steady game (bright pickup 3.1 -> 6.0) and 3-10 dB less top-end noise removed under notes. Variants that halve the sparkles also halve the gain: the pick click and the GPU bursts share the same bins. Not judged by ear yet; it may read as more bite or more fizz.

albums.title: Noise canceller v0.12: hum tracking under notes (A/B)
albums.description: Two overnight builds for Travis to A/B. Hum tracking gives each hum tone its own narrow listener (a 2 Hz-wide filter around the tone), so the hum keeps being measured while you play, with notes that sit right on a hum line detected and held off; it also tracks pitch drift. It's behind an A/B switch, default off. Tonal protection (telling sustained guitar partials from random GPU bursts by phase) was prototyped and dropped: in the top end the two don't separate, so it would have dulled the guitar. Harness tests: synthetic hum and buzz changes over real in-game interference, plus clean takes.
albums.result: Hum tracking: hum +20 dB at 60 Hz removed under notes 18.1 -> 38.6 dB, 120/180 Hz 8/5 -> 24/25, new buzz 7.8 -> 20.5; guitar unchanged, notes tuned next to hum lines kept, CPU +2%, off = bit-identical to v0.11. Tonal protection failed: GPU noise coherence 0.32-0.44 vs guitar top end 0.5-0.6, not separable. Not yet tried on the real rig.

albums.title: Noise canceller v0.10: no more Learn button
albums.description: Travis's idea: drop the manual Learn step. A second of noise is enough, and the output stays muted while the plugin learns, so you never hear it. With no profile the plugin listens for a second with no guitar in it (no pick attack, a steady level, nothing ringing out, not right after an even riff), learns from it, then opens. albums.title: Noise canceller v0.9.4: gaps that catch up
albums.description: Travis heard 'a gap that doesn't catch up' and sparkles. Cause: with nobody playing, the note detector sometimes still said 'playing', so the gap got the gentle under-note cut and nothing re-tuned. albums.title: Noise canceller v0.9.3: following the noise while playing
albums.description: Where the sparkles came from: following the interference only in gaps between notes left the filter stale while playing through a change, like leaning toward the PC. v0.9.3 measures the interference level every 1.5 ms from the 2.5-10 kHz median, notes or not; on real takes the guitar moves that by at most 0.4 dB. albums.title: EMI noise canceller: why maxed-out settings sound best
albums.description: Travis found his best settings at the slider extremes (noise threshold 12, cut between notes 60, cut under notes 40, tone tracking 0.5 ms): guitar rings out and decays naturally with no gate and the noise is gone. Investigation of why.
albums.result:
1. A high-gain amp is a huge compressor. Leftover interference between notes, measured after a stand-in high-gain chain, below playing level: no plugin 0.8 dB, 35/35 defaults 8.5 dB, his settings 21.4 dB. It takes about 60 dB on the DI for gaps to be silent after the amp.
2. The guitar's energy is concentrated: 95.5% of it sits in frequency bins more than 12 dB above the interference, so a 12 dB threshold keeps the body of every note and removes everything between the harmonics (20.3 dB cut under notes vs 13.3 at threshold 2).
3. The cost: only 8% of the guitar's energy above 2.5 kHz clears 12 dB, so the DI's top end drops about 25 dB; after the amp the tone measurably changes (spectral difference 8.2 vs 4.3 dB). Heavy distortion regenerates highs and the cab cuts above about 5 kHz, so it reads as smoother, less fizzy distortion: partly tone shaping. Likely too dark on clean tones, which suggests separate high-gain and clean presets.
4. Decays survive because the note detector holds 'playing' through them and lets go only once a note has sunk into the interference.
5. Tone tracking 0.5 ms really doubles hum refit speed (only ~9 base tones, so it stays stable).

albums.description: Travis's tuned settings locked in as defaults, plus a fix for the learned profile being lost on a bypass toggle.

Not ready; parked on a branch, v0.9.1 stays current.

albums.title: EMI noise canceller: Acon-style noise statistics vs the filter's ceiling
albums.description: Test of Acon DeNoise 2's 'dynamic noise profile' idea on real GPU/VRM interference: does tracking the noise frame by frame, instead of one average profile, keep more of the guitar under notes?

images.title: what limits the filter under notes
images.label: Noise canceller

albums.result:
Measured on real in-game interference + 5 clean guitar takes, at ~14 dB interference cut under notes (guitar above 2.5 kHz kept).
Average profile (current): -11.2 dB. Realistic dynamic estimators (reference-band level tracking, burst on/off profiles, 90th-percentile profile): -11.1 to -15.1 dB, no gain.
Even perfect per-frame knowledge of the interference (cheat): -8.7 dB, only +2.5 dB. The filter's decision-directed smoothing already averages over frames.
Ideal mask (cheat: knows which bins are guitar): -2.6 dB at ~11 dB cut, the same at any window from 1.5 to 23 ms. The limit is knowing where the guitar is, not resolution or latency.

albums.title: EMI noise canceller v0.8: static filter and note detector
albums.description: REAPER JSFX prototype. A new static filter turns the GPU/VRM bursts down (hard between notes, gently under notes), and the note detector now also listens at 80-700 Hz.
albums.result:
Run through the real JSFX in ysfx on real in-game interference mixed with 5 clean guitar takes.
Interference removed, between notes / under notes: spectral mode (+6 ms, default) 25.0 / 14.1 dB; zero-latency mode 22.7 / 12.2 dB; v0.7 tones only 3.5 / 0 dB.
Cost under notes: guitar above 2.5 kHz drops ~11 dB. Note decays kept within 0.6 dB.
Note detector: caught 68-93% of real playing with the game running (v0.7 caught 0%), with 0% false alarms.
Checks passed: synthetic regression identical to v0.7.1 with the static filter off; spectral path reconstructs bit-exactly with 256 samples of reported latency; output after a project save/reload matches a straight run to -147 dB; v0.7 projects still load (tones only until re-learn); no NaN/Inf in any run.
Fixed along the way: a subtractive-bandpass zero-latency design that only reached 5-11 dB, and a band split that shifted the low end's phase as bands opened (replaced with a Linkwitz-Riley split).
Not yet judged by ear through the amp sim; the display's live-cut overlay compiles but hasn't been seen on screen.

albums.title: EMI noise canceller: what the PC interference is
albums.description: Guitar DI recorded with the game running, hands off the strings. Target: an EMI denoiser for GPU coil whine, VRM switching noise and PC-fan induction, first in the chain before the amp sim.
albums.result:
Interference enters through the pickups: a volume-knob swell next to the PC (idle desktop) gave -93 dBFS with the knob at 0 and -64 dBFS with it up. In-game it reaches -38 dBFS RMS, about 55 dB above the clean floor.
Tonal part, cancellable by the v0.7 tone canceller: mains harmonics from 60 to 2640 Hz and a ~177 Hz buzz at game launch. A small share of the energy.
About 90% of the energy (2.5-10 kHz) is GPU/VRM bursts: ~140 per second, 2-3 ms each, ringing the pickup near 5.5 kHz. No narrow tones and no repeating waveform.
Failed: 'close enough' cancellation of the bursts removes at most 0.9-1.4 dB even with perfect timing, gain and polarity. Bursts match each other for only ~0.5 ms and their spacing jitters 1.5-2.5 ms.
Conclusion: the tones can be phase-cancelled; the bursts can only be reduced from a single input.
albums.label: Noise canceller
